teaching.task: # Year 11 Chemistry M2 V16: Avogadro's law and molar volume. Why do equal gas volumes contain equal amounts at the same conditions? (design)
teaching.causalExplanation: The same, about two point four times ten to the twenty-two particles in each. To see why, think about how much room the particles themselves take up. A mole of liquid nitrogen fills about thirty-five millilitres. Let it boil, and at room conditions the same particles fill about twenty-five litres, around seven hundred times the space. So a gas is almost all empty space, and the particles take up well under one percent of the jar. That's why their size hardly matters. So what does set the volume? Gas particles never stop moving, and every time one hits a wall, it pushes on it. All those pushes add up to the gas's pressure, the push on each square metre of wall. A gas spreads out until its push on the walls matches the push from outside, here a hundred kilopascals. So the volume depends on how often the particles hit the walls, and how hard each hit is. Now the surprise. Hydrogen molecules are sixteen times lighter than oxygen molecules, so you might expect them to push less. But at the same temperature, lighter molecules move faster, about four times faster here. Each hit is only a quarter as hard, but there are four times as many hits each second. The two effects cancel. So at the same temperature, every gas particle, heavy or light, pushes on the walls just as hard on average.

Nitrogen is chosen because it is the main gas in air and is a liquid students may have seen in demonstrations; water is the site's example but is not a gas at 25 °C.
- **Reason 2, what sets the volume (Revision 2 visual).** Wall hits make pressure; a gas behind a movable boundary expands or shrinks until its push matches the outside push (100 kPa). A gas in a rigid lidded jar simply fills the jar and can have a pressure different from outside; the jars are kept only for the equal-volume comparison at the stated conditions. Suggest adding: "At the same temperature, lighter particles move faster but each hit pushes less, so every particle contributes the same average pressure."

- **Learner question (route wording kept).** "Why do equal gas volumes contain equal amounts at the same conditions?" The answer, in order: the particles' size hardly matters, because gas is almost all empty space (2); volume is set by the push of wall hits against the outside pressure (3); at one temperature every particle pushes equally, whatever its mass (4); so equal volumes, temperatures and pressures mean equal numbers (5); which gives one molar volume per set of conditions (6, 7) and volume ratios for gas reactions (8).

- **Reason 3, why mass doesn't matter (adds the missing half of the site's account; site note 2).** At the same temperature, the particles' average kinetic energy is the same, so lighter particles move faster: H₂ is about 16 times lighter than O₂ and moves about 4 times faster on average. Spoken without "kinetic energy" (one grey tag "same temperature: same average energy of motion"). The numbers are exact consequences of ½mv² being equal (author note c).

The particles' own volume is "well under one percent" (a liquid's volume overstates the molecules' own volume, so the true share is smaller still).
(c) Mass independence: at temperature T, average translational kinetic energy is the same for every gas, so m⟨v²⟩ is equal; pressure from N particles is proportional to N m⟨v²⟩. (d) Real gases at 25 °C and 100 kPa: molar volumes of common gases differ from 24.79 by well under 1% (CO₂ about 0.5% smaller). Not spoken beyond "very closely".
(e) Molar volumes: 8.314 × 273.15 ÷ 100 = 22.71; 8.314 × 298.15 ÷ 100 = 24.79; 24.79 ÷ 22.71 = 1.0916 ≈ 298.15 ÷ 273.15 = 1.0915 (m2-v18's Charles's law; not spoken). 22.4 L mol⁻¹: 0 °C and 101.325 kPa.
(f) Syringe: 2.00 × 10⁻³ × 24.79 = 0.0496 L = 49.6 mL; 4.00 × 10⁻³ × 24.79 = 99.2 mL.
(g) Worked example: 4.96 ÷ 24.79 = 0.2001 → 0.200 mol; 4.96 ÷ 22.71 = 0.2184 → 0.218 mol.

scenes.teachingReason: So what does set the volume? Gas particles never stop moving, and every time one hits a wall, it pushes on it. So the volume depends on how often the particles hit the walls, and how hard each hit is.
